claims.text: The premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by the interplay of atomic-scale chemical disorder and lattice strain.
Chemical disorder modulates energy barriers for surface and bulk atomic rearrangements.
Lattice strain modulates energy barriers for surface and bulk atomic rearrangements.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during heating.
Chemical disorder creates local variations in bonding strength.
Chemical disorder creates local variations in atomic coordination.
Lattice strain alters the energy landscape for atomic mobility.
Chemical disorder and lattice strain influence the onset of surface atomic rearrangements associated with premelting.
Chemical disorder and lattice strain influence the bulk melting transition.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will have a broader premelting temperature range than pure nickel nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will undergo bulk melting later than pure nickel nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
The predicted broader premelting range and delayed bulk melting arise from stabilizing effects of chemical disorder and lattice strain.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles having chemical-disorder and lattice-strain characteristics similar to those of the target particles.
The hypothesis is limited to particle sizes at which surface effects dominate thermal behavior, exemplified as particles smaller than 100 nm.
Prior study of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is too limited to predict precise temperature ranges or relative effect magnitudes.
